questions.stem: How is net profit related to gross profit in a trading business?
options: net profit is always exactly half of the gross profit for the period
net profit is gross profit less the owner's drawings for the period
net profit is gross profit plus other revenue less all other expenses
net profit is gross profit plus the cost of goods sold for the period
questions.explanation: Gross profit is net sales less cost of goods sold; net profit then adds other revenue and deducts operating expenses such as wages and rent. Drawings are not an expense, so they do not affect net profit.

questions.stem: Profitability refers to a business's ability to:
options: survive in the long term given how its assets are financed by debt and equity
convert its inventory into cash as quickly as possible
earn a satisfactory profit compared with its sales or the resources invested
pay its debts as they fall due in the short term
questions.explanation: Profitability compares profit with sales, assets or equity. The ability to pay short-term debts is liquidity.

questions.stem: Liquidity refers to a business's ability to:
options: earn a high return on the owner's investment
reduce its cost of goods sold each year
attract more customers than its competitors
meet its short-term debts as they fall due
questions.explanation: Liquidity is about having enough cash, or assets that will soon become cash, to pay current liabilities on time. A business can be profitable but illiquid if its cash is tied up.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware had net sales of $250,000 and cost of goods sold of $160,000. Using gross profit ÷ net sales × 100, what is its gross profit ratio?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = 250,000 − 160,000 = $90,000, and 90,000 ÷ 250,000 = 36%. 64% is cost of goods sold as a share of sales.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware's net profit was $22,500 on net sales of $250,000. Using net profit ÷ net sales × 100, what is its net profit ratio?
questions.explanation: 22,500 ÷ 250,000 = 9%, so the business keeps 9 cents of each sales dollar as profit. 25% would be the result of dividing by average owner's equity of $90,000 rather than by sales.

questions.stem: Net profit was $22,500. Owner's equity was $80,000 at the start of the year and $100,000 at the end. Using net profit ÷ average owner's equity × 100, what is return on owner's equity?
questions.explanation: Average equity = (80,000 + 100,000) ÷ 2 = $90,000, and 22,500 ÷ 90,000 = 25%. Using closing equity gives 22.5% and opening equity gives 28.1%.

questions.stem: Inventories were $18,000 at the start of the year and $22,000 at the end, and cost of goods sold was $146,000. Using average inventories ÷ cost of goods sold × 365, what is the turnover of inventories?
options: 45 days
50 days
7.3 days
55 days
questions.explanation: Average inventories = (18,000 + 22,000) ÷ 2 = $20,000, and 20,000 ÷ 146,000 × 365 = 50 days. Using closing inventories gives 55 days, and 7.3 is the number of times per year.

questions.stem: Accounts receivable were $14,000 at the start of the year and $18,000 at the end, and net credit sales were $146,000. Using average accounts receivable ÷ net credit sales × 365, what is the turnover of accounts receivable?
options: 45 days
35 days
9.1 days
40 days
questions.explanation: Average accounts receivable = (14,000 + 18,000) ÷ 2 = $16,000, and 16,000 ÷ 146,000 × 365 = 40 days. Using closing receivables gives 45 days and opening receivables 35 days.

questions.stem: A business's inventory turnover fell from 8 times a year to 5 times a year. What is the most likely effect?
options: accounts payable will fall, because suppliers are always paid sooner when stock moves slowly
more cash is tied up in slow-selling stock, weakening liquidity and risking obsolete goods
inventory is selling faster, so cash is being received from customers sooner than before
gross profit must have risen, because holding more inventory always increases profit
questions.explanation: Turning inventory over fewer times means each item takes longer to sell, tying up cash and increasing storage costs and the risk of goods becoming outdated. Faster selling would be shown by more times a year.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware's accounts receivable turnover is 40 days, but it offers 30-day credit terms. Which statement best describes the situation?
options: the business is selling too little on credit, so the ratio will rise until sales increase
customers are taking longer than the terms allow, slowing cash inflows and raising the risk of bad debts
customers are paying faster than required, so the business could safely extend its credit terms to 60 days
the business is paying its suppliers late, which is why its receivables turnover is high
questions.explanation: On average customers pay 10 days late, which delays cash and may signal accounts that will not be collected. Accounts payable turnover measures payments to suppliers, not receipts from customers.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware's accounts receivable turnover improved from 45 days to 28 days, with 30-day credit terms. What does this indicate?
options: customers now take longer to pay, so the risk of bad debts has increased
the business has stopped selling on credit altogether, so its sales must have fallen sharply
the business now pays its suppliers faster than the agreed credit terms
customers now pay within the terms, so cash comes in sooner and liquidity improves
questions.explanation: Fewer days means receivables are collected faster, on average within the 30-day terms, which strengthens cash flow. The ratio concerns customers, not suppliers.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware's gross profit ratio fell from 40% to 33%, although it sold more units than the year before. What is the most likely explanation?
options: wages and rent rose faster than sales, cutting the profit on each sale
the owner took more drawings, which are deducted before gross profit
more sales were on credit, and credit sales are excluded from gross profit
heavy discounting or higher purchase costs reduced the profit on each sale
questions.explanation: The gross profit ratio depends only on selling prices and the cost of goods sold, so a fall alongside higher volume points to discounting or dearer stock. Wages, rent and drawings do not affect gross profit, and credit sales are included in net sales.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware is considering extending its credit terms from 30 to 60 days to attract trade customers. What is the most likely effect?
options: sales will fall, but cash will be received from customers sooner, improving liquidity
there will be no effect on cash, because credit terms only affect profit
bad debts will fall, because customers have longer to find the money
sales and profit may rise, but cash will come in later and liquidity may weaken
questions.explanation: Longer terms may win more sales, but receipts are delayed and the risk of non-payment usually rises with the time a debt is outstanding. Credit decisions involve a trade-off between profitability and liquidity.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of credit customers failing to pay their accounts?
options: liabilities fall, because customers' debts are owed to the business
inventory increases, because unpaid goods are automatically returned to the business by customers
cash inflows fall, causing liquidity problems, and any bad debts reduce profit
net profit rises, because the business keeps the goods it sold
questions.explanation: Unpaid accounts mean cash the business expected does not arrive, making it harder to pay its own debts, and writing off bad debts adds an expense. The goods have already been sold and are not returned.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Kitchenware regularly pays its suppliers well after the due date. Which consequence is most likely?
options: suppliers may stop offering credit or take legal action, harming future supply
suppliers will offer larger discounts to encourage the business to keep buying
the business's net profit will rise, because late payment is a form of revenue
the business's inventory turnover will improve, because stock is paid for later
questions.explanation: Not paying suppliers on time damages relationships and the business's credit reputation, and suppliers may demand cash on delivery or recover the debt legally. Late payment does not create revenue.

questions.stem: A business has a low gross profit for the year. Which is a likely cause?
options: wages and rent rose sharply during the year
the owner took unusually large cash drawings during the year
the business borrowed a large amount from the bank
selling prices are too low or the cost of the goods bought is too high
questions.explanation: Gross profit depends only on net sales and cost of goods sold, so it is affected by pricing, purchase costs, discounting and inventory losses. Wages and rent affect net profit, and drawings and loans affect neither.

questions.stem: A sole trader reports a net loss for the year. What is the effect on the Statement of Financial Position?
options: owner's equity is unchanged until the loss is paid
owner's equity decreases by the amount of the loss
liabilities increase by the amount of the loss
current assets increase by the amount of the loss
questions.explanation: A net loss reduces capital in the owner's equity section. It is not a liability, and it must be funded from assets or by borrowing, so it often weakens liquidity too.

questions.stem: The owner of Kookaburra Kitchenware takes significant cash drawings during the year. What is the main effect on the business?
options: cash and owner's equity fall, leaving less to pay debts and fund operations
net profit falls, because drawings are reported as an operating expense
liabilities rise, because the owner now owes the drawings back to the business
gross profit falls, because drawings are added to the cost of goods sold
questions.explanation: Drawings are not an expense, so profit is unaffected, but they reduce cash and capital. Heavy drawings can leave the business short of cash to pay suppliers or replace assets.

questions.stem: Two identical businesses each earned net profit of $30,000 and started the year with owner's equity of $60,000. One owner's drawings left closing equity at $56,000; the other's heavy drawings left it at $40,000. Using average equity, how do their returns on owner's equity compare?
options: about 52% and 60%; the higher figure reflects equity run down by drawings, not better performance
about 52% and 60%; the higher figure shows the second business is managed more efficiently
both are 50%, because each earned the same net profit on the same opening equity
about 54% and 75%; the higher figure means the second business has better liquidity
questions.explanation: 30,000 ÷ 58,000 = 51.7% and 30,000 ÷ 50,000 = 60%. The second ratio is higher only because heavy drawings shrank equity, which also drained cash, so it signals weaker liquidity rather than better performance.

questions.stem: Before paying a supplier's invoice, Kookaburra Kitchenware matches it with the purchase order and the delivery docket. What is the main purpose of this control?
options: to check the customer's credit history before allowing a credit sale
to pay only for goods that were ordered and actually received, at the agreed price
to make sure the supplier is paid as early as possible so that the business can earn interest
to calculate the gross profit ratio for the period on each purchase
questions.explanation: Matching the three documents prevents paying for goods not ordered, not delivered or charged at the wrong price, protecting both profit and cash. Credit checks apply to customers, not suppliers.

questions.stem: Which internal control over accounts receivable would most directly reduce bad debts?
options: checking credit references and setting a credit limit before granting credit
allowing every new customer unlimited credit to encourage more sales
sending statements of account only once at the end of the year
letting the salesperson who makes each sale also write off unpaid debts
questions.explanation: Assessing customers before giving credit and limiting how much they can owe reduces the chance and size of losses. Infrequent statements and combining selling with writing off debts weaken control.

questions.stem: Why should the employee who looks after the storeroom not also keep the inventory records?
options: it means inventory no longer needs to be recorded at cost price
it lets the business claim extra GST credits on its purchases
separating custody from recording makes it harder to steal goods and hide the loss
it allows the business to avoid counting its inventory at the end of the year, saving staff time
questions.explanation: If one person both holds the goods and keeps the records, they could remove stock and alter the records to cover it. Separation of duties means one person's work checks another's.

questions.stem: Regular stocktakes at Kookaburra Kitchenware keep revealing losses. How does this affect profitability and liquidity, and what should be done?
options: losses raise costs and reduce cash from sales; restrict storeroom access and investigate
losses raise gross profit and cash; increase inventory levels so losses matter less
losses affect neither profitability nor liquidity, so no action is needed
losses only affect liquidity; increase the bank overdraft to cover them
questions.explanation: Lost inventory is a cost with no sales revenue, so profit falls and the cash spent on the goods is never recovered. Controls such as restricted access, security and investigation address the cause.

questions.stem: What is the likely effect on profitability and liquidity of a business holding far more inventory than it needs?
options: there is no effect, because inventory is an asset and assets are always good
cash is tied up and storage costs rise, and some goods may have to be marked down
cash increases because suppliers pay the business to store their goods
gross profit rises, because holding large inventory levels always reduces the cost of goods sold
questions.explanation: Excess inventory uses cash that could pay debts, adds storage and insurance costs, and risks obsolescence and markdowns that reduce profit. Holding more stock does not reduce the cost of what is sold.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet graph best shows gross profit and net profit for each month of the year?
options: a table of the year's closing balances with no graph
a line graph with one line for gross profit and one for net profit
a single pie chart showing the year's total gross profit
a single pie chart showing each month's net profit as a separate slice of the year
questions.explanation: A two-series line or column graph shows each measure month by month and the gap between them, which is the other expenses. A pie chart shows shares of one total and does not show change over time.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, which graph best shows how the owner's equity, liabilities and assets of a business have changed over five years?
options: a scatter plot of liabilities against the number of staff
a single pie chart of last year's revenue items
a column graph with a group of columns for each year
a single pie chart of the five years' total assets
questions.explanation: Grouped or stacked columns allow each element to be compared across the years. A pie chart shows parts of one total at one time, so it cannot show change over time.

questions.stem: In a vertical analysis of Kookaburra Kitchenware's Statement of Profit or Loss, wages of $45,000 on net sales of $250,000 are shown as:
options: 18% of net sales
5.6% of net sales
45% of net sales
82% of net sales
questions.explanation: 45,000 ÷ 250,000 = 18%, meaning 18 cents of each sales dollar is spent on wages. Vertical analysis lets items be compared across years or businesses of different sizes.

questions.stem: Vertical analysis shows that Kookaburra Kitchenware's advertising rose from 3% to 7% of net sales, while net sales were unchanged. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: advertising grew without increasing sales, so its effectiveness should be reviewed
the extra advertising clearly caused a large increase in sales during the year
advertising fell in dollar terms, because its percentage of sales has changed
the net profit ratio must have risen because advertising is now a larger share
questions.explanation: With sales flat, a higher percentage means more was spent on advertising for no extra revenue, reducing the net profit ratio. The owner should evaluate whether the campaign is worth continuing.
